title: A Sign Law for Entropy Drift under Sampler Mismatch in RLVR

paper.title: A Sign Law for Entropy Drift under Sampler Mismatch in RLVR
paper.abstract:
Abstract Entropy in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) moves up or down depending on choices that should be neutral, such as whether over-length responses are masked or counted as failures.
We trace this to sampler mismatch , where rollouts are drawn with top- k k /top- p p truncation or at a temperature the learner does not apply, and prove that a constant advantage shift then changes the entropy of a softmax policy, at first order and in expectation, with a sign fixed by the sampler: positive shifts sharpen the policy under any sampler whose likelihood ratio to the policy increases with token probability, including top- k k , top- p p , min- p p , and temperatures below one, and flatten it under flatter samplers.
In group-based RLVR with token-level losses, the baseline-controlled part of this drift is set by the token-weighted net advantage , which masking and failing over-length responses can push to opposite signs; the remainder, a covariance between advantages and the sampler’s sharpness gap, can feed back over long horizons.
On a 2B model, the entropy slope is linear in shifts of the net advantage under truncated sampling and indistinguishable from flat under exact sampling, and token-level importance ratios leave 98% of the drift.
In 100-step runs, a net-zero baseline only delays an entropy explosion that exact sampling does not show, a fixed positive shift delays it further, and a baseline weighted by the sharpness gap keeps entropy stable without changing the learner.
On a 9B reasoning model over ten steps, the uncorrected rule loses held-out accuracy, whereas zeroing the net advantage or renormalizing the learner gains 8.2 and 8.8 points over it, with no held-out effect under exact sampling.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1 : Change in entropy of a 2B model on a fixed probe set under three advantage rules (mean over 3 seeds; bands show the range). Under truncated sampling (top- k k 20, top- p p 0.95), masking over-length responses ( N > 0 N>0 ) lowers entropy and counting them as failures ( N < 0 N<0 ) raises it, with the net-zero baseline ( N = 0 N=0 ) in between. With exact sampling, or with truncated sampling and a learner that renormalizes over the sampled support, the three rules nearly coincide. Policy entropy is the most closely watched health signal in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and it fails in both directions. When it collapses, the policy stops exploring and accuracy plateaus ( Cui et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) ; when it explodes, responses degrade and training can diverge ( The Microsoft AI Team, 2026 ; Hugging Face TRL contributors, 2026 ) . Yet the direction of entropy often hinges on choices that seem unrelated to it. Figure 1 shows an example: in otherwise identical runs, masking over-length responses drives entropy down while counting them as failures drives it up, and with exact sampling the two runs are indistinguishable. Most accounts of entropy dynamics assume on-policy rollouts, where entropy follows the covariance between advantages and log-probabilities ( Cui et al., 2025 ) and responds to clipping ( Park et al., 2025 ) , and where baseline invariance makes a constant advantage shift harmless ( Williams, 1992 ) . Masking or failing over-length responses mainly changes the balance between positive and negative advantages, so on-policy theory offers no reason for the two to push entropy in opposite directions. In practice, rollouts are often not drawn from the policy that the learner differentiates: engines sample with top- k k , top- p p , or min- p p truncation, or at a temperature the learner does not apply ( Section 5 ). Under such sampler mismatch , a constant advantage shift adds a drift toward or away from the sampler ( Le Roux, 2016 ; Le Roux et al., 2025 ; Marek & Ryabinin, 2026 ) , which recent systems remove by replaying the sampling mask ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; The Microsoft AI Team, 2026 ; Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2026 ; Cognition, 2026a ) or centering the score ( Marek & Ryabinin, 2026 ) . For a fixed full-support behavior policy, a higher baseline makes the limit policy deterministic ( Arnal et al., 2025 ) ; for truncation, a torchtitan pull request argues in words that the drift sharpens or flattens the policy and does not average out over a group ( PyTorch torchtitan contributors, 2026 ) , and SCOPE-RL reports a reversal across temperatures ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . What is missing is a sign statement for general samplers derived from the policy; the batch quantity that controls the drift in group-based RLVR, where advantages within a group already sum to zero; and an account of what each correction removes. We show that the drift moves entropy with a sign fixed by the sampler, and that a single batch statistic sets its baseline-controlled part. Our sign law ( Theorem 1 ) states that under any sampler sharper than the policy, including top- k k , top- p p , min- p p , and temperatures below one, a positive advantage shift lowers entropy at first order and a negative shift raises it; flatter samplers, such as temperatures above one, reverse both. The shift that a token-level loss applies is the token-weighted net advantage N g N_{g} of each group, which equals Cov ⁡ ( r , L ) / L ¯ \mathrm{Cov}(r,L)/\bar{L} under a group-mean baseline and gains a nonnegative term under masking ( Table 3 ). Because long responses fail more often, failing them makes N N negative and pushes entropy up, whereas masking makes N N positive in our runs and pushes it down. A second term, from failed responses visiting less confident prefixes, does not depend on the baseline; on real batches it is the smaller one, but the gap it depends on grows as the policy moves away from a sharper sampler, so over long horizons it feeds back on itself. Setting N = 0 N=0 , as the length-weighted baseline of OPO ( Hao et al., 2025 ) does, removes the net-advantage term; weighting the baseline by each response’s gap cancels the two terms against each other; renormalizing the learner over the sampled support removes the whole drift and coincides with score centering; token-level importance ratios only rescale it. On a 2B model, the entropy slope is linear in shifts of N N under truncated sampling; the difference between masking and failing grows with the measured sharpness of the sampler across six samplers and reverses sign at temperature 1.2; and it shrinks to 2–4% when the learner is renormalized or applies the sampling temperature, but stays at 98% under exact importance ratios. Sequence-mean aggregation, which zeroes N N for failing but not for masking, brings failing to the level of the net-zero baseline and leaves masking unchanged, as predicted. In 100-step runs the net-zero baseline only delays an entropy explosion that exact sampling does not show, and the gap-weighted baseline keeps entropy stable ( Figures 3 and 4 ); the theory predicts signs and comparisons within a rule, not absolute sizes. On a 9B reasoning model under truncated sampling, zeroing N N raises held-out accuracy by 8.2 points over ten steps (95% interval 4.2–12.1 over training seeds) and renormalizing the learner by 8.8, while under exact sampling the rules do not differ. Our contributions are: • A sign law for every sampler sharper or flatter than the policy ( Sections 3.1 and 3.2 ). • A split of the mismatch drift into a net-advantage term and a gap covariance, and what each correction removes ( Sections 3.3 and 3.4 ). • Controlled evidence on Qwen-family models at 2B and 9B, including 100-step runs and controls, a replication on OLMo-3-7B, and a survey of practice ( Sections 4 and 5 ).

sections.heading: Over-length responses.
sections.text: Responses that reach the generation limit have no verifiable answer, and pipelines handle them in one of three ways that we use throughout. Mask , a form of overlong filtering ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , assigns them zero reward when computing the baseline and then excludes them from the loss; Fail assigns zero reward and trains on them; Pen additionally lowers the reward of long completed responses with a linear over-length penalty ( Yu et al., 2025 ) .

sections.text: Both mismatch terms scale with the gap, and the gap depends on the policy. A drift away from a sharper sampler therefore tends to enlarge the gap and accelerate itself, most strongly when the kept set has a fixed size as under top- k k , while a drift toward it shrinks the gap until the drift stops. Because D cov D_{\mathrm{cov}} raises entropy in our runs, zeroing N N removes the initial push but leaves a term that can start this loop; Section 4.5 observes both outcomes.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We test the predictions of Section 3 in turn, ending with accuracy at 9B and 100-step runs at 2B.

sections.heading: Models and data.
sections.text: We use Qwen3.5-2B (non-thinking mode, released checkpoint), MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B ( Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2026 ) , and, as a second model family, OLMo-3-7B-Instruct ( Team Olmo, 2025 ) . The 9B experiments fork from step 20 (weights and optimizer state) of a run that reproduces the configuration of a public RLVR run of this model; that run sampled with top- k k 20 and top- p p 0.95 and did not renormalize the learner. Prompts come from the MATH training set ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) (7,496 problems with verifiable answers, graded by math-verify); 750 problems are held out from all training, including the reproduced run before the 9B fork, and all evaluation and probe prompts are drawn from them.

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: Unless a rule says otherwise, all runs use the same trainer: groups of 8 responses, a group-mean baseline without standard-deviation normalization, prompt-mean aggregation, AdamW with learning rate 10 − 6 10^{-6} , gradient clipping at 1, no KL or entropy terms, and one optimizer step per batch. The 2B runs use 16 groups per step and a 2,048-token limit for 15 steps, or 100 steps in Section 4.5 ; the 9B runs use 32 groups per step and an 8,192-token limit for 10 steps. Rewards are binary for 2B; the 9B runs add the Pen over-length penalty.

sections.heading: Samplers and rules.
sections.text: We compare truncated sampling (top- k k 20, then top- p p 0.95, at T = 1 T=1 ), top- p p 0.99 and top- p p 0.8 alone, exact sampling, and untruncated sampling at T = 0.7 T=0.7 and T = 1.2 T=1.2 , with a learner at T = 1 T=1 . As corrections we test support renormalization (recomputed in the learner; Appendix C ), token-level importance ratios against the truncated distribution computed by the learner, either exact or inside the standard clipped objective, and a learner that applies the sampling temperature. Advantage rules are Mask , Fail , Fail + NZ , and Fail + GapW for 2B, with sequence-mean aggregation and a fixed advantage shift as further controls, and Fail + Pen with and without NZ for 9B, where we also run Fail + Pen with a renormalized learner; the 2B runs log the gap of every sampled response, computed by the learner under the sampling rule.

sections.heading: Measuring entropy.
sections.text: Before every update we compute the mean full-softmax token entropy of the current policy on a fixed probe set, one response for each of 64 held-out prompts, sampled once from the initial policy and scored by teacher forcing, so the measurement does not depend on batch composition. The entropy slope of a run is the least-squares slope of this quantity over steps. Runs with the same seed see the same prompts and sampling seeds, so arms differ in one factor; we use two or three seeds per 2B cell and four per 9B cell, and treat the seed as the unit of replication.

sections.heading: 4.2 The net advantage predicts the direction of entropy
sections.text: On rollouts of the 9B model at the fork point, the mean gap under top- k k 20 and top- p p 0.95 is 4.4 × 10 − 3 4.4\times 10^{-3} per token, larger on completed incorrect responses than on correct ones ( 5.5 5.5 against 4.0 × 10 − 3 4.0\times 10^{-3} ), which makes D cov D_{\mathrm{cov}} raise entropy. A pure positive shift lowers the entropy of held-out prompts at both scales, along the raw gradient and the Adam step, and with exact sampling the effect falls to 4% at 9B and within 6% at 2B ( Table 6 ), which also bounds the finite-sample effects that remain without mismatch. sections.heading: 5 Sampler Mismatch in Practice
sections.text: We surveyed 19 trainers in 18 RL frameworks and three inference engines at fixed commits, and 123 technical reports and public recipes ( Appendix E ). Mismatch enters through framework defaults (ROLL samples with T = 0.95 T=0.95 , top- p p 0.7, and top- k k 50 without dividing by T T ), inherited generation configs, and recipes; of the 55 reports and recipes that disclose their training sampler, 7 (13%) train with uncorrected truncation or temperature mismatch, and corrections landed in several frameworks only during 2026. In single 300-step runs of a 1.5B model, final entropy was 3.63 with top- p p 0.95 and top- k k 512, 0.69 with top- p p 1.0, and 0.54 after renormalization ( Hugging Face TRL contributors, 2026 ) . These findings suggest four practices: remove the mismatch on the learner’s side, by renormalizing over the sampled support or centering the score on the post-truncation distribution (which vLLM returns only on request) and by applying the sampling temperature in the learner; when only the advantages can be changed but the learner’s logits are available, use GapW rather than a net-zero baseline or a fixed shift; do not rely on token-level importance ratios under truncation, which left 98% of the drift; and log N N and the mean gap, whose growth signals the feedback of Section 3.3 .

sections.heading: Entropy dynamics in RLVR.
sections.text: Entropy collapse is addressed with clip-higher ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , entropy-targeted objectives ( Decugis et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) , and adaptive controllers ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) , some of which reweight positive and negative samples and so change N N . On-policy, entropy follows the covariance between advantages and log-probabilities ( Cui et al., 2025 ) ; it responds to clipping ( Park et al., 2025 ) and to log-probability-dependent advantages ( Petrenko et al., 2026 ) , and positive-only reinforcement collapses it ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) . The per-token term Φ \Phi of Equation 3 is the entropy polarity of Zhang et al. (2026) , and our gap is its expectation under the sampler. SCOPE-RL ( Wang et al., 2025 ) shows that the effect of positive samples reverses between low and high sampling temperatures, a case of the sign law.

sections.heading: Baselines and mismatch.
sections.text: Without importance correction, a constant baseline adds a KL ( μ ∥ π ) \mathrm{KL}(\mu\|\pi) gradient whose direction depends on the sign of the mean advantage ( Le Roux, 2016 ; Le Roux et al., 2025 ) , a constant shift acts as pessimism under partial coverage ( Cao et al., 2026 ) , and baselines matter even on-policy through finite-sample effects ( Chung et al., 2021 ) . AsymRE ( Arnal et al., 2025 ) shows that for a fixed full-support behavior policy a baseline above the behavior value makes the limit policy deterministic, and observes faster entropy loss in LLMs; under truncation the same push away from the sampler fills the discarded tail and raises entropy, so the direction depends on the sampler, which Theorem 1 characterizes for ordered samplers. Marek & Ryabinin (2026) formalize the drift for quantization, kernel, and staleness mismatch, propose score centering, and note that group centering does not remove it; Proposition 1 identifies what remains and how it moves entropy, and Han & Hu (2026) give a gradient-level mean–covariance split of the same kind and an estimand that restores shift invariance under regularized importance sampling. GapW has the form of variance-optimal baselines, which weight rewards by the squared score norm ( Greensmith et al., 2004 ; Hao et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026b ) , with weights set by the drift instead. OPO, which zeroes the net advantage, keeps entropy similar to GRPO with a matched sampler ( Hao et al., 2025 ) and is reported to keep the training–inference KL low ( Cognition, 2026b ) ; balanced aggregation identifies the sign–length coupling behind the net advantage and removes it ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ) . Mismatch drift can compound because the sampler tracks the trainer ( Marek & Ryabinin, 2026 ; Jiang, 2026 ) ; the torchtitan description of top- p p flattening as ending once tail tokens enter the nucleus ( PyTorch torchtitan contributors, 2026 ) matches our top- p p control, and cooler sampling without correction collapses ( Pan, 2026 ) .

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: When rollouts come from a sampler sharper or flatter than the policy, the baseline stops being free: a constant advantage shift moves entropy with a sign fixed by the sampler; in group-based RLVR the shift is the token-weighted net advantage, which masking and failing push to opposite signs, and the remaining gap covariance feeds back over long horizons unless a gap-weighted baseline or a renormalized learner cancels it. The theory is first order and predicts signs, not sizes; the long runs use a 2B model and few seeds, and the 9B runs ten steps.

sections.heading: Impact Statement
sections.text: This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of machine learning. It identifies a silent source of instability in reinforcement learning for language models and gives practitioners a diagnostic and simple corrections, which can make training runs more reliable and reduce compute wasted on failed runs. We do not foresee negative societal consequences specific to this work beyond those of the field.

sections.text: We built a synthetic RLVR task with 8 problems and a tabular autoregressive policy whose context is (problem, position, running sum mod 5, a derailment flag); responses are correct if they stop with an allowed residue, and a derailing token leads to an over-length response, so over-length responses are long and low-confidence, as in our language-model data. sections.heading: Data.
sections.text: The pool contains 7,496 math problems with verifiable answers. We hold out 750 problems from training; the held-out evaluation set is a fixed random subset of 300 of them, and the 64 probe prompts are drawn from that subset. The fixed evaluation set contains 32 problems, each sampled 8 times; 3 of them are also probe prompts.

sections.heading: Samplers.
sections.text: Rollouts are generated by vLLM. Truncated sampling applies top- k k 20 and then top- p p 0.95 at T = 1 T=1 . Support renormalization recomputes the kept set from the learner’s logits with the same rule and renormalizes the learner’s log-probability of the sampled token over the kept set joined with that token; the sampled token falls outside the recomputed set for about 0.06% of tokens, because of numerical differences between engine and learner. For T = 0.7 T=0.7 and T = 1.2 T=1.2 , no truncation is applied and the learner computes log-probabilities at T = 1 T=1 .

sections.heading: Probe set and entropy.
sections.text: The probe set contains one response per prompt for 64 held-out prompts, sampled once from the starting policy with truncated sampling. Before every update we compute, by teacher forcing, the full-softmax entropy at every response token and average over tokens. Pure-shift derivatives on a probe set sampled with exact sampling agree with those on the truncated probe set ( Appendix D ).

sections.heading: Grading and statistics.
sections.text: Answers are extracted from the final \boxed{} and graded with math-verify. All 9B evaluations, including those of runs trained with exact sampling, use truncated sampling so that arms are compared under the same evaluation protocol. For accuracy we treat the training seed as the unit: we compute the paired difference between rules for each seed (arms with the same seed share prompts and sampling seeds) and report the mean, a t t -based 95% interval with 3 degrees of freedom, and a two-sided paired t t -test. sections.heading: Reports and recipes.
sections.text: We collected 123 technical reports, open recipes, and papers that describe RLVR training of language models, and classified each by its training rollout sampler: (A) truncation without correction, (B) truncation with support renormalization or score centering, (C) no truncation and matched temperature, (D) temperature not applied by the learner, and (E) not disclosed. Eighteen entries were collected specifically from frameworks with truncating defaults and are excluded from the prevalence count. The remaining 105 entries split into 5 A, 2 B, 46 C, 2 D, and 50 E; most large-model technical reports are E, so the 13% rate among the 55 disclosed entries describes public recipes, not production pipelines. Commonly cited sampling settings of open models (e.g., top- p p 0.95, top- k k 20) are evaluation settings and were not counted as training settings. Earlier releases had truncating defaults that the table, which uses current commits, does not show: recipes from TRL v0.16–0.17, EasyR1 v0.3, and Unsloth’s GRPO notebooks truncate with top- k k 50, top- p p 0.99, or min- p p 0.1.

sections.heading: Appendix G Stale Rollouts and Clipping
sections.text: Asynchronous pipelines sample from an older policy π old \pi_{\mathrm{old}} . We added a rollout lag of k k steps to the tabular simulation of Appendix B , here with SGD on the logit table (learning rate 50), and compared vanilla policy gradient with importance ratios against π old \pi_{\mathrm{old}} and PPO clipping. • Without importance ratios, a constant shift pulls the policy back toward π old \pi_{\mathrm{old}} when N > 0 N>0 and pushes it away when N < 0 N<0 , in 99.5–100% of steps. Its entropy effect is feedback on the most recent entropy trend rather than an independent source, so it has no universal sign at first order; over many steps with a fixed behavior policy, a baseline above the behavior value instead drives the limit policy to a deterministic one ( Arnal et al., 2025 ) . • Importance ratios with clipping remove the stale component: under exact sampling the dose-response slope of entropy on N N is − 0.002 -0.002 to + 0.005 +0.005 for lags 2–32. They leave the truncation component intact: under truncated sampling the slope is − 0.290 -0.290 , − 0.301 -0.301 , and − 0.246 -0.246 for lags 2, 8, and 32, against − 0.297 -0.297 without lag. Ratios against π old \pi_{\mathrm{old}} correct for staleness because π old \pi_{\mathrm{old}} is the distribution that generated the tokens up to truncation; they cannot correct truncation because π old \pi_{\mathrm{old}} is not the sampler. Clipping has a related effect when a batch is used for several updates. With ratio ρ = π / π old \rho=\pi/\pi_{\mathrm{old}} and clip range ϵ \epsilon , the expected gradient of a constant advantage c c is c ​ π ​ ( U ) ​ ( q U − π ) c\,\pi(U)(q_{U}-\pi) , where U U is the set of tokens not clipped for the sign of c c ; clipping therefore acts like a truncation of the support to U U , and a constant shift again moves entropy, with a sign that depends on which tokens are clipped ( Park et al., 2025 ) . This offers one route by which shifting all advantages, as positive-only versus negative-only reinforcement does, changes entropy in pipelines with several clipped updates per batch ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , whereas our single-update exact-sampling runs show almost no effect of a shift of the same size ( Table 6 ).

In group-based RLVR with token-level losses, the baseline-controlled part of this drift is set by the token-weighted net advantage , which masking and failing over-length responses can push to opposite signs; the remainder, a covariance between advantages and the sampler’s sharpness gap, can feed back over long horizons. On a 2B model, the entropy slope is linear in shifts of the net advantage under truncated sampling and indistinguishable from flat under exact sampling, and token-level importance ratios leave 98% of the drift. In 100-step runs, a net-zero baseline only delays an entropy explosion that exact sampling does not show, a fixed positive shift delays it further, and a baseline weighted by the sharpness gap keeps entropy stable without changing the learner. On a 9B reasoning model over ten steps, the uncorrected rule loses held-out accuracy, whereas zeroing the net advantage or renormalizing the learner gains 8.2 and 8.8 points over it, with no held-out effect under exact sampling. With exact sampling, or with truncated sampling and a learner that renormalizes over the sampled support, the three rules nearly coincide. Policy entropy is the most closely watched health signal in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and it fails in both directions. When it collapses, the policy stops exploring and accuracy plateaus ( Cui et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) ; when it explodes, responses degrade and training can diverge ( The Microsoft AI Team, 2026 ; Hugging Face TRL contributors, 2026 ) . Yet the direction of entropy often hinges on choices that seem unrelated to it. Figure 1 shows an example: in otherwise identical runs, masking over-length responses drives entropy down while counting them as failures drives it up, and with exact sampling the two runs are indistinguishable. Most accounts of entropy dynamics assume on-policy rollouts, where entropy follows the covariance between advantages and log-probabilities ( Cui et al., 2025 ) and responds to clipping ( Park et al., 2025 ) , and where baseline invariance makes a constant advantage shift harmless ( Williams, 1992 ) . Masking or failing over-length responses mainly changes the balance between positive and negative advantages, so on-policy theory offers no reason for the two to push entropy in opposite directions. In practice, rollouts are often not drawn from the policy that the learner differentiates: engines sample with top- k k , top- p p , or min- p p truncation, or at a temperature the learner does not apply ( Section 5 ). Under such sampler mismatch , a constant advantage shift adds a drift toward or away from the sampler ( Le Roux, 2016 ; Le Roux et al., 2025 ; Marek & Ryabinin, 2026 ) , which recent systems remove by replaying the sampling mask ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; The Microsoft AI Team, 2026 ; Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2026 ; Cognition, 2026a ) or centering the score ( Marek & Ryabinin, 2026 ) . For a fixed full-support behavior policy, a higher baseline makes the limit policy deterministic ( Arnal et al., 2025 ) ; for truncation, a torchtitan pull request argues in words that the drift sharpens or flattens the policy and does not average out over a group ( PyTorch torchtitan contributors, 2026 ) , and SCOPE-RL reports a reversal across temperatures ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . What is missing is a sign statement for general samplers derived from the policy; the batch quantity that controls the drift in group-based RLVR, where advantages within a group already sum to zero; and an account of what each correction removes. We show that the drift moves entropy with a sign fixed by the sampler, and that a single batch statistic sets its baseline-controlled part. Our sign law ( Theorem 1 ) states that under any sampler sharper than the policy, including top- k k , top- p p , min- p p , and temperatures below one, a positive advantage shift lowers entropy at first order and a negative shift raises it; flatter samplers, such as temperatures above one, reverse both. The shift that a token-level loss applies is the token-weighted net advantage N g N_{g} of each group, which equals Cov ⁡ ( r , L ) / L ¯ \mathrm{Cov}(r,L)/ ar{L} under a group-mean baseline and gains a nonnegative term under masking ( Table 3 ). Because long responses fail more often, failing them makes N N negative and pushes entropy up, whereas masking makes N N positive in our runs and pushes it down. A second term, from failed responses visiting less confident prefixes, does not depend on the baseline; on real batches it is the smaller one, but the gap it depends on grows as the policy moves away from a sharper sampler, so over long horizons it feeds back on itself. Setting N = 0 N=0 , as the length-weighted baseline of OPO ( Hao et al., 2025 ) does, removes the net-advantage term; weighting the baseline by each response’s gap cancels the two terms against each other; renormalizing the learner over the sampled support removes the whole drift and coincides with score centering; token-level importance ratios only rescale it. On a 2B model, the entropy slope is linear in shifts of N N under truncated sampling; the difference between masking and failing grows with the measured sharpness of the sampler across six samplers and reverses sign at temperature 1.2; and it shrinks to 2–4% when the learner is renormalized or applies the sampling temperature, but stays at 98% under exact importance ratios. Sequence-mean aggregation, which zeroes N N for failing but not for masking, brings failing to the level of the net-zero baseline and leaves masking unchanged, as predicted. In 100-step runs the net-zero baseline only delays an entropy explosion that exact sampling does not show, and the gap-weighted baseline keeps entropy stable ( Figures 3 and 4 ); the theory predicts signs and comparisons within a rule, not absolute sizes. On a 9B reasoning model under truncated sampling, zeroing N N raises held-out accuracy by 8.2 points over ten steps (95% interval 4.2–12.1 over training seeds) and renormalizing the learner by 8.8, while under exact sampling the rules do not differ. In single 300-step runs of a 1.5B model, final entropy was 3.63 with top- p p 0.95 and top- k k 512, 0.69 with top- p p 1.0, and 0.54 after renormalization ( Hugging Face TRL contributors, 2026 ) . These findings suggest four practices: remove the mismatch on the learner’s side, by renormalizing over the sampled support or centering the score on the post-truncation distribution (which vLLM returns only on request) and by applying the sampling temperature in the learner; when only the advantages can be changed but the learner’s logits are available, use GapW rather than a net-zero baseline or a fixed shift; do not rely on token-level importance ratios under truncation, which left 98% of the drift; and log N N and the mean gap, whose growth signals the feedback of Section 3.3 . 6 Related Work Entropy dynamics in RLVR. Entropy collapse is addressed with clip-higher ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , entropy-targeted objectives ( Decugis et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) , and adaptive controllers ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) , some of which reweight positive and negative samples and so change N N . On-policy, entropy follows the covariance between advantages and log-probabilities ( Cui et al., 2025 ) ; it responds to clipping ( Park et al., 2025 ) and to log-probability-dependent advantages ( Petrenko et al., 2026 ) , and positive-only reinforcement collapses it ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) . The per-token term Φ \Phi of Equation 3 is the entropy polarity of Zhang et al. (2026) , and our gap is its expectation under the sampler. SCOPE-RL ( Wang et al., 2025 ) shows that the effect of positive samples reverses between low and high sampling temperatures, a case of the sign law. Baselines and mismatch. Without importance correction, a constant baseline adds a KL ( μ ∥ π ) \mathrm{KL}(\mu\|\pi) gradient whose direction depends on the sign of the mean advantage ( Le Roux, 2016 ; Le Roux et al., 2025 ) , a constant shift acts as pessimism under partial coverage ( Cao et al., 2026 ) , and baselines matter even on-policy through finite-sample effects ( Chung et al., 2021 ) . AsymRE ( Arnal et al., 2025 ) shows that for a fixed full-support behavior policy a baseline above the behavior value makes the limit policy deterministic, and observes faster entropy loss in LLMs; under truncation the same push away from the sampler fills the discarded tail and raises entropy, so the direction depends on the sampler, which Theorem 1 characterizes for ordered samplers. Marek & Ryabinin (2026) formalize the drift for quantization, kernel, and staleness mismatch, propose score centering, and note that group centering does not remove it; Proposition 1 identifies what remains and how it moves entropy, and Han & Hu (2026) give a gradient-level mean–covariance split of the same kind and an estimand that restores shift invariance under regularized importance sampling. GapW has the form of variance-optimal baselines, which weight rewards by the squared score norm ( Greensmith et al., 2004 ; Hao et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026b ) , with weights set by the drift instead. OPO, which zeroes the net advantage, keeps entropy similar to GRPO with a matched sampler ( Hao et al., 2025 ) and is reported to keep the training–inference KL low ( Cognition, 2026b ) ; balanced aggregation identifies the sign–length coupling behind the net advantage and removes it ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ) . Mismatch drift can compound because the sampler tracks the trainer ( Marek & Ryabinin, 2026 ; Jiang, 2026 ) ; the torchtitan description of top- p p flattening as ending once tail tokens enter the nucleus ( PyTorch torchtitan contributors, 2026 ) matches our top- p p control, and cooler sampling without correction collapses ( Pan, 2026 ) . 7 Conclusion When rollouts come from a sampler sharper or flatter than the policy, the baseline stops being free: a constant advantage shift moves entropy with a sign fixed by the sampler; in group-based RLVR the shift is the token-weighted net advantage, which masking and failing push to opposite signs, and the remaining gap covariance feeds back over long horizons unless a gap-weighted baseline or a renormalized learner cancels it. The theory is first order and predicts signs, not sizes; the long runs use a 2B model and few seeds, and the 9B runs ten steps. Impact Statement This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of machine learning. It identifies a silent source of instability in reinforcement learning for language models and gives practitioners a diagnostic and simple corrections, which can make training runs more reliable and reduce compute wasted on failed runs.
